title: Emerald Tech - Zero Trust On‑Prem Network Sandbox Review
summary: Redwood and Emerald Tech reviewed Private/on‑prem deployment security posture: network isolation, ingress/egress controls, KMS integration (BYOK), RBAC/SSO flow, audit log routing and retention, and SOC2 artefacts. Agreed pilot scope and follow ups for network diagrams, test plan for egress allowlist, and KMS proof-of-concept.
topics: Egress allowlist and firewalling for on-prem runtime
Audit log ingestion to SIEM / immutable retention
SSO/SAML & SCIM provisioning and RBAC mapping
action_items: Tom Ellis: Share internal network topology + VLAN/VRF diagrams by 2026-01-21
Claire Patel: Send Redwood security packet (SOC2, ISO certs, pen test summary) by 2026-01-16
Jordan Mehta: Prepare KMS BYOK integration notes + example Terraform by 2026-01-23
Rafael Kim: Provide egress ACL testbed subnet and contact for firewall admin by 2026-01-20
next_steps: Schedule hands-on pilot kickoff (2 week window) - target week of 2026-01-27
Redwood to propose test plan for egress allowlist and latency perf checks
Customer to validate SSO metadata (SAML) and provide IdP test account
transcript:
[00:00] Claire Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know this is a packed agenda so we'll run through the sandbox topology and then deep dive on security controls.
[00:18] Anika Rao: Yep, thanks Claire, appreciate it. We sketched out our air‑gapped subnet and want to make sure Redwood can live in the same DMZ without creating lateral access.
[00:33] Jordan Mehta: Cool, we're expecting that. Quick note - when we say 'private' for Redwood we mean the control plane can be customer‑managed and the runtime nodes live inside your VPC / on-prem cluster, isolated.
[00:48] Tom Ellis: So, the main ask is ingress/egress discipline. We need a default deny approach outbound and only allow specific egress destinations. How does Redwood handle outbound TLS to model stores or telemetry?
[01:05] Jordan Mehta: By default our runtime only opens outbound connections to configured endpoints. For on‑prem we support NAT gateway routing through an egress bastion or through customer managed proxy. We can do allowlist by FQDN and IPs; note DNS can complicate things if your proxy rewrites.
[01:24] Tom Ellis: Right, DNS egress leakage is a concern. Do you support forced proxy or TLS intercept options?
[01:31] Luis Ortega: We don't do TLS interception within the runtime. The recommended approach is an outbound proxy that terminates TLS and mTLS to external services or an egress gateway that enforces ALPN/hostname allowlist.
[01:45] Priya Nair: How about latency impacts if we're routing through an egress proxy vs direct peering to Redwood nodes in our colo?
[01:54] Jordan Mehta: There's measurable added RTT through a proxy — typically 10-30ms depending on path — but for generation workloads that is usually acceptable; for strict p95 latency SLOs we recommend dedicated peering or colocated runtimes.
[02:10] Anika Rao: Can we talk keys — BYOK? We require customer‑managed keys and rotation via our HSM.
[02:18] Jordan Mehta: Yes, we support customer KMS integration. Options: TPM/HSM backed KMS via KMIP, or cloud KMS BYOK where you provide key and Redwood can reference via IAM. For on‑prem, we can integrate with vault or an HSM appliance using PKCS#11 or KMIP.
[02:35] Tom Ellis: Do you have a KMS proxy pattern? I want to make sure keys never leave our HSM raw.
[02:40] Jordan Mehta: We support envelope encryption — the data keys are generated and wrapped by your HSM, Redwood never stores unwrapped key material. We also support HSM signing for key rotation audits.
[02:52] Rafael Kim: For audit logs, we need wire‑level logging and immutable retention for 7 years. Can Redwood ship logs to our Splunk or S3 with WORM?
[03:02] Claire Patel: Yes, we can stream audit events via syslog, HTTPS, or direct S3 ingestion; S3 WORM is supported for compliance. We also provide structured audit events (user, operation, resource, request id).
[03:15] Tom Ellis: How granular are those events? Do we get request/response token counts, model version, and prompt hash?
[03:23] Jordan Mehta: We emit request metadata including model id, model version, prompt hash (optionally redacted), token counts, latency, and auth principal. Response bodies can be excluded or redacted per config.
[03:34] Anika Rao: About RBAC + SSO — we use SAML 2.0 with SCIM for provisioning. We'd like role mapping to our groups (ops, security, dev). Can Redwood map groups to roles?
[03:45] Luis Ortega: Yes SAML + SCIM supported. We do group claim mapping and can set fine‑grained roles: read-only, operator, admin, auditor. We can also integrate with OIDC providers if you prefer.
[03:58] Priya Nair: Is there justification logging for role elevation and who approved it?
[04:02] Jordan Mehta: We have audit trails for RBAC changes with the acting principal and timestamp; for approvals we can integrate with your ticketing system or capture the approval metadata in the event.
[04:12] Tom Ellis: On SOC2/ISO — we need the latest certs and pen test summary. Do you have a SOC2 Type II report and ISO27001?
[04:20] Claire Patel: Yes, we'll share the redacted SOC2 Type II report and ISO27001 certificate. We'll include the latest pen test exec summary and remediation timeline.
[04:29] Anika Rao: Good. For network isolation, we're leaning to microsegmentation with explicit allow rules between the runtime and our model storage. We also want to control egress to telemetry endpoints (no telemetry to internet).
[04:41] Jordan Mehta: You can configure telemetry sinks to point to internal endpoints only. For messaging between services we recommend mutual TLS and mTLS certs pinned to service identities.
[04:50] Rafael Kim: Can Redwood run with no external DNS? Our environment doesn't allow outbound DNS queries except to internal resolvers.
[04:58] Luis Ortega: That's fine, as long as the runtime is preconfigured with IPs or internal DNS resolvable hostnames. For host-based allowlists we can accept IP ranges in the runtime config.
[05:08] Tom Ellis: What about software updates and patching for the on‑prem runtime? We need control over when updates are applied in production pockets.
[05:15] Claire Patel: For private deployments we support controlled update windows and can provide signed releases. There is an option for air‑gapped update bundles you can pull into an isolated repo and sign.
[05:28] Priya Nair: Is there an offline install? Some of our sites are quasi‑airgapped.
[05:32] Jordan Mehta: Yes, we have an offline installer tarball plus an operator image you can deploy to your cluster. For air‑gapped we do a verified signature and provide a verification tool.
[05:43] Anika Rao: Let's detail egress: we want an outbound allowlist limited to specific Redwood control-plane IPs and S3 endpoints for model artifacts. We also want to prevent accidental DNS tunneling.
[05:55] Jordan Mehta: We can provide a minimal set of egress IPs and FQDNs required for the runtime, and we recommend using egress firewall rules plus DNS egress monitoring for tunneling. We also recommend TLS inspection at the proxy if you need DPI, but note that breaks end-to-end TLS so you must evaluate security tradeoffs.
[06:13] Tom Ellis: For the pilot can you provide a smaller IP range and a deterministic port list?
[06:18] Jordan Mehta: Yes, we'll provide an allowlist for the pilot; we usually use outbound 443 and 5222 for control-plane heartbeat, and certain ports for metrics ingestion (443 or 9080 depending on sink). Exact ports will be in the config spec we send.
[06:33] Rafael Kim: Heartbeat frequency and connection pattern matter — will the runtime keep persistent connections or do ephemeral connections per request?
[06:40] Luis Ortega: Mostly persistent control plane websockets for signaling. For model pulls it's HTTP(s) with conditional requests. Persistent connections reduce connection churn and help with NAT table stability.
[06:52] Anika Rao: We require mTLS for all control plane comms. Is that supported with customer certs?
[06:57] Jordan Mehta: Supported — we accept mTLS with customer CA bundles. You can provide an internal CA and we will trust that for the runtime's control plane mutual TLS.
[07:08] Tom Ellis: Logging retention and immutability — you mentioned S3 WORM. Can you guarantee retention enforcement if Redwood manages the bucket?
[07:16] Claire Patel: If Redwood manages the bucket, we can enable object lock and retention policies; however customers often prefer to manage the bucket for stronger control. Either way we can provide verifiable write-once policies and audit logs of writes.
[07:29] Priya Nair: We also want to ensure time sync and consistent timestamps for forensic purposes.
[07:33] Jordan Mehta: Runtime nodes run chrony/ntp and we can centralize logs with the timezone normalized to UTC. We include the node timestamp and ingest timestamp in each event for correlation.
[07:44] Anika Rao: A potential blocker — our legal team requires that no PII leaves the VPC unless explicitly permitted. For embedding jobs, can you avoid sending embeddings to Redwood cloud?
[07:54] Luis Ortega: For Private/on‑prem deployments embeddings and model tokens remain local. For hosted features we provide config to disable telemetry and to keep data local. For any optional services that need external processing we require explicit opt-in.
[08:07] Tom Ellis: What about model updates? If Redwood pushes model patches, do prompts ever leave to external stores?
[08:13] Jordan Mehta: Model updates are pulled from your artifact repo or from a sealed artifact store you control. If you choose Redwood's managed model catalog, then those pulls could occur to the public internet, but for private we can mirror the artifacts internally.
[08:24] Anika Rao: On the topic of pen tests, do you allow us to run internal red team exercises against the runtime? We need to do authenticated vulnerability scans prior to production cutover.
[08:33] Claire Patel: Yes, we have a coordinated vulnerability disclosure and pre-production testing program. We provide test scope and a point of contact, and we've done many customer led scans with NDA in place.
[08:45] Priya Nair: Can we get the SBOM and component list for the runtime? That's a must for our SBOM policy.
[08:51] Jordan Mehta: We'll provide an SBOM and container image digests. For the pilot we'll share a reduced SBOM and full SBOM once NDA is in place.
[09:01] Tom Ellis: Any hard requirements on DNS or NTP? You said internal DNS is fine — do we need DNS SRV records?
[09:08] Luis Ortega: No SRV required; plain A/AAAA records or internal resolvables are fine. The runtime expects DNS resolution for hostnames you provide. For strict environments, you can use hostfile mappings.
[09:20] Anika Rao: Let's map out the pilot acceptance criteria. We propose: 1) runtime deploys in sandbox VPC, 2) egress allowlist enforced with no outbound traffic to the internet outside allowlist, 3) KMS BYOK integration, 4) audit logs ingest to Splunk, 5) SSO via SAML.
[09:36] Claire Patel: That scope is reasonable. For egress enforcement we'll work with Rafael and Tom to validate traffic in the test period. We'll also provide a minimal perf test (100 concurrent requests) to measure latency overhead.
[09:49] Tom Ellis: For RBAC, ensure that the 'auditor' role cannot call admin APIs or extract raw outputs.
[09:55] Jordan Mehta: Correct — the auditor role is read-only and we have scoped operations to prevent data exfiltration. We'll demo role enforcement in the pilot.
[10:03] Rafael Kim: Firewall rules: do you need any inbound from Redwood to our cluster?
[10:08] Jordan Mehta: Inbound only if you expose a webhook or if you're running a hybrid control plane that uses inbound callbacks. Typically we recommend the runtime initiate outbound connections to the control plane. If you require inbound, we can use a reverse tunnel model.
[10:20] Anika Rao: Reverse tunnels are not ideal for us, prefer outbound-only.
[10:24] Luis Ortega: Outbound-only is fully supported and the recommended pattern.
[10:28] Priya Nair: About monitoring, we want visibility into token usage and cost per request. Does Redwood export token-level metrics?
[10:35] Claire Patel: Yes token counts and cost metrics can be forwarded to your observability stack. We also provide per-route breakdowns in the console. For private deployments the console can be deployed as read-only for your teams.
[10:48] Tom Ellis: Any known gotchas with mTLS on older load balancers? We have some vintage F5s.
[10:55] Jordan Mehta: Older proxies sometimes choke on ALPN or SNI if they don't support TLS 1.3. We recommend validating ALPN and cipher suite compatibility; we can provide a compatibility matrix.
[11:08] Anika Rao: What about secrets management for runtime config? We use HashiCorp Vault.
[11:13] Luis Ortega: We have a Vault integration pattern: runtime fetches secrets via instance auth and uses short lived tokens. We also support sealed secrets as a fallback.
[11:22] Rafael Kim: For the pilot, who is the contact for firewall rule changes?
[11:26] Tom Ellis: That would be me and Rafael; Rafael will be the admin who applies ACLs.
[11:31] Claire Patel: Great, we'll include Rafael in the pilot kickoff invite.
[11:35] Anika Rao: Any recommendations on microsegmentation? We're thinking of isolating the runtime into its own VRF and only permitting the management plane from our admin subnets.
[11:43] Jordan Mehta: That aligns with best practice. Additionally, use host level policies to limit outbound by process identity and disable unnecessary egress from the runtime host.
[11:55] Priya Nair: Ok let's cover the final deliverables again. Claire?
[11:59] Claire Patel: We'll send the security packet (SOC2, ISO, pen test summary), the pilot allowlist + config spec, the KMS integration guide, and a proposed pilot schedule. Jordan will provide the KMS Terraform snippets.
[12:13] Tom Ellis: I'll send our network diagrams and a test subnet for the pilot.
[12:17] Rafael Kim: I'll provide firewall admin contact and test credentials for the proxy.
[12:22] Anika Rao: One quick question — for data residency we have EU-only requirement for some workloads. Is region pinning available?
[12:30] Claire Patel: Yes, for private we support regional pinning and you can ensure runtime lives in specific datacenters or on-prem clusters; we'll capture that in the contract.
[12:39] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone.
[12:42] Jordan Mehta: Thanks — we'll follow up with the docs.
[12:45] Claire Patel: End of call.
notes: Customer emphasized egress allowlist/pilot as gating item
Redwood to provide SOC2 and ISO artifacts quickly
KMS BYOK and SAML/SCIM provisioning are critical success criteria
